elements.quote: introduction: this paper updates and summarizes the current evidence informing rehabilitation of patients with coVid-19
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the report as a systematic review by stating it "updates and summarizes the current evidence" and the title explicitly labels it a "rapid living systematic review".

elements.quote: from this edition, we improved the quality assessment using the Joanna briggs institute checklists for observational studies and the cochrane risk of bias tool for randomized-controlled clinical trials (rcts).
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the tools used to assess risk of bias.

elements.quote: papers were categorized according to study design, research question, coVid-19 phase, limitations of functioning of rehabilitation interest, and type of rehabilitation service involved.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the methods used to synthesize the results (categorization).

elements.quote: Twenty-five, out of 3699 papers, were included. They were three RCTs, 13 cross-sectional studies and nine cohort studies. ... all study participants were coVid survivors and 48% of studies collected information on participants 6 months or longer after coVid-19 onset.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (25), the study types, and summarizes relevant study characteristics (participants were COVID survivors, follow-up duration).

elements.quote: Twenty studies reported data on symptom prevalence (N.=13) or disease natural history (N.=7); and five studies reported intervention effectiveness at the individual level.
elements.reason: The abstract summarizes the main findings/outcomes.

elements.quote: This third edition still provides a narrative synthesis of findings, as a meta-analysis is not applicable due to the high heterogeneity of the studies.
elements.reason: No meta-analysis was conducted.

The review did not compare groups in a way that requires reporting a direction of effect for a specific intervention comparison in the abstract; it is a descriptive synthesis of observational and RCT data.

elements.quote: the most frequent risks of bias for rcts concerned weaknesses in allocation concealment, blinding of therapists, and lack of intention-to-treat analysis. Most analytical studies failed to identify or deal with confounders, describe or deal with dropouts or eventually perform an appropriate statistical analysis .
elements.reason: The abstract summarizes important limitations regarding risk of bias.

elements.quote: There is a need for good quality intervention efficacy and effectiveness studies to complement the rapidly expanding evidence from observational studies.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an interpretation of the results and implications.
The abstract does not mention the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide the register name and registration number.

elements.quote: A high proportion of SARS-CoV-2 patients survive infection but the prevalence of chronic sequelae and resulting disability is increasing. These survivors need clinical management and rehabilitation to facilitate good health outcomes. ... To date, the ClinicalTrials.gov website 2 of the National Library of Medicine has registered more than 6400 clinical studies targeting the epidemiology and management of COVID-19, but only 245 studies (188 of which are ongoing) address rehabilitation in COVID-19 survivors.
elements.reason: The text describes the current state of knowledge regarding COVID-19 survivors needing rehabilitation and highlights the uncertainty/gap in evidence regarding rehabilitation specifically, noting that while many studies exist for COVID-19, few address rehabilitation.

elements.quote: The best available research evidence is required to inform management and rehabilitation decisions, interventions, and health systems for COVID-19 survivors with adverse clinical sequelae. Further evidence is warranted to estimate the resources needed to plan for setting appropriate and adequately delivered post-acute and long-term rehabilitation services.
elements.reason: The text explicitly explains the importance and need for the review, stating that evidence is required to inform management and rehabilitation decisions and to plan for rehabilitation services.

elements.quote: This rapid living systematic review on rehabilitation and COVID-19 was initiated in April 2020 as a component of the Cochrane Rehabilitation REH-COVER action. 3 Since its inception, it has been updated monthly, with the most recent update leading to a total of 319 papers up to April 30 th , 2021.
elements.reason: The review identifies itself as an update of a living systematic review, citing previous editions and the ongoing nature of the work.
This is a broad systematic review of rehabilitation evidence for COVID-19, not a review of a specific intervention's mechanism of action.
The review is a broad synthesis of evidence on rehabilitation needs and outcomes, not a review of a specific complex intervention requiring a logic model.
